Summary of LDM seminar.pptx
=================================

Title: Latent Diffusion Models - A Survey on Foundations, Variants, and Web-Scale Deployments
Presented by: Leo Antony (S7 AD, JEC23AD034)
Guide: Divya Konikkara
Date: 10/09/2026

Overview
--------
The presentation is a seminar survey on Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs), covering their foundations, major variants, and deployments at web scale.

Index / Structure
-----------------
01. Introduction - Why generative modeling matters and where LDMs fit.
02. Previous Generative Models - Feed-forward networks and (pixel-space) diffusion models.
03. Latent Diffusion Models - Diffusion performed in a smarter, compressed latent space.
    (Section 3 also discusses visual meta / conditioning aspects.)
Section 3 theme: "Diffusion, but in a Smarter Space" - LDMs run the diffusion process in a
lower-dimensional latent space produced by an autoencoder rather than on raw pixels,
making training and sampling far more efficient.

Key Ideas
---------
- Generative modeling aims to learn the data distribution and sample new data.
- Earlier models (feed-forward networks, pixel-space diffusion) are expensive at high resolution.
- LDMs add a perceptual compression stage (encoder/decoder) so diffusion operates in latent space.
- This yields high-quality image generation with reduced compute.
- Variants extend the core approach, and the method scales to web-scale deployments.

Conclusion
----------
LDMs are an efficient, scalable family of generative models; performing diffusion in a latent
space balances quality and computational cost and underpins many modern image generators.

(Source: extracted text from the 24-slide LDM seminar deck.)

DETAILED SUMMARY: LDMseminar Presentation
========================================================================

Title: Latent Diffusion Models
Subtitle: A Survey on Foundations, Variants, and Web-Scale Deployments
Author: Leo Antony (S7 AD, Register No. JEC23AD034)
Guide: Divya Konikkara
Date: 10/09/2026
Seminar: LDM Seminar 2026

------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. OVERVIEW
------------------------------------------------------------------------
This seminar presentation surveys Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs), covering
their conceptual foundations, variants, and large-scale (web-scale)
deployments. The deck is approximately 20-24 slides, organised into five
sections. Per the instructor's guidance, the focus is conceptual foundations
and there is no separate results chapter. Sections 02 and 04 carry most of
the technical depth.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. STRUCTURE / INDEX
------------------------------------------------------------------------
01 - Introduction
02 - Foundations (latent space, VAE, diffusion modeling)
03 - (Variants / methods)
04 - Technical depth (architecture, conditioning, training)
05 - Web-Scale Deployments / Conclusion

------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY CONCEPTS COVERED
------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Latent Diffusion Models operate in a compressed latent space rather than
  the full-resolution pixel space, making diffusion far more efficient.
- Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are used to encode inputs into a latent
  representation and reconstruct them back. A VAE maps each input to a
  probability distribution, making the latent space continuous, smooth and
  sampleable - exactly what diffusion models require.
- Reconstructing images directly at pixel level is problematic: with
  multiple plausible outputs (e.g. faces), an MSE loss pushes the network
  toward the mean of possibilities instead of one sharp reconstruction.
- The MSE = ... formulation is used to compute reconstruction differences
  during training.
- Datasets referenced include the FFHQ (Flickr-Faces-HQ) dataset, shown as
  Figure 1, used to illustrate the face reconstruction problem.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. PRACTICAL / SEMINAR NOTES
------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Preview the five sections of the deck in order.
- Emphasise that the focus is conceptual foundations - there is no separate
  results chapter per the instructor's guidance.
- Total deck is roughly 20 slides; sections 02 and 04 carry most of the
  technical depth.

REPORT: LDM Seminar Presentation
=====================================

Source file: C:\Users\USER\Downloads\LDM seminar.pptx (13.2 MB, 24 slides)
Title: Latent Diffusion Models — A Survey on Foundations, Variants, and Web-Scale Deployments
Author: Leo Antony (S7 AD, JEC23AD034)
Guide: Divya Konikkara
Date: 10/09/2026

-------------------------------------
OVERVIEW
-------------------------------------
This presentation is a technical seminar on Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs),
covering their conceptual foundations, the history of prior generative models,
the LDM architecture, and how LDMs are deployed as web-scale services.
It is organised into four main sections (plus introduction), with sections 02
and 04 carrying the most technical depth.

-------------------------------------
SECTION 1 — INTRODUCTION (Slides 1-3)
-------------------------------------
- LDMs generate high-quality images by iteratively denoising a random signal.
  Instead of operating on raw pixels, they work inside a compressed latent space
  produced by a trained autoencoder.
- Two phases:
    * Forward process — adds Gaussian noise as a fixed Markov chain.
    * Reverse process — a U-Net learns to denoise step by step.
- Advantages over previous models:
    * ~48x cheaper than pixel-space diffusion at the same quality.
    * Sharper than VAEs, which tend to produce blurry samples.
- Powers Stable Diffusion, SDXL, and Stable Video Diffusion.

-------------------------------------
SECTION 2 — PREVIOUS GENERATIVE MODELS (Slides 4-9)
-------------------------------------
1) Feed-Forward Network
   - A plain feed-forward CNN trained on FFHQ faces with MSE/L2 loss to
     super-resolve 16x16 inputs back to high-resolution faces.
   - Application: recovering recognisable identity from tiny low-res inputs
     (CCTV, thumbnails, degraded photos).
   - Failure mode: outputs are blurry, averaged "ghosts" of all plausible
     faces — the MSE loss pushes the network toward the mean of possibilities
     instead of a single sharp reconstruction.

2) Diffusion Models
   - A diffusion model learns to produce data (images, audio, video) by
     learning to reverse a gradual noising process.
   - Instead of mapping noise -> image in one shot (like feed-forward), it
     breaks generation into many small denoising steps.

   Phase 1 — Forward Process (Noise Addition):
     * A Markov chain of T steps adds a small amount of Gaussian noise at every
       step, controlled by a variance schedule beta_1 ... beta_T.
     * Each step depends only on the previous one (Markov property).
     * As t -> T, x approaches an isotropic Gaussian (data becomes pure noise).
     * The process is fixed (not learned), so any intermediate x can be sampled
       directly from x0 in one step — essential for efficient training.

   Phase 2 — Reverse Process (Learning to Denoise):
     * The reverse process learns: "Given noisy image x_t, what noise should I
       remove to get closer to the original image?"
     * The U-Net takes noisy image x_t and timestep t as inputs and predicts the
       added noise eps(x_t, t).
     * Actual noise vs predicted noise is compared using MSE.
     * The MSE is used to compute gradients via backpropagation; U-Net weights
       are updated with an optimizer such as Adam, reducing prediction error.

-------------------------------------
SECTION 3 — LATENT DIFFUSION MODELS (Slides 10-20)
-------------------------------------
Why we need LDMs:
  - Massive memory footprint: the U-Net must process 512x512x3 activation maps
    at every layer and every step; GPU memory explodes with resolution.
  - Slow iterative sampling: 100-1000 reverse steps x per-step U-Net inference
    = minutes-to-hours per image; infeasible for interactive web use.
  - Wasted redundancy: natural images are highly compressible; most pixel-level
    information is high-frequency texture, not semantic content.

The Latent Space (VAE):
  - A Variational Autoencoder compresses data (images, audio, text) into a
    small, structured latent space and reconstructs it back.
  - A VAE maps each input to a probability distribution, making the latent
    space continuous, smooth, and sampleable — exactly what diffusion needs.
  - Encode: encoder produces mean (mu) and log-variance (log sigma^2); sample a
    latent z = mu + sigma * eps, where eps ~ N(0, I).
  - Decode: decoder converts z back into an image x_hat = D(z).

How LDMs Use the VAE:
  - Role 1 (Perceptual compression): encoder compresses pixel space -> latent
    space (one-time, before diffusion begins).
  - Role 2 (Final reconstruction): decoder translates the denoised latent z0
    back into a viewable image (one-time, after diffusion ends).
  - The diffusion U-Net runs entirely in latent space — it never touches raw
    pixels. The autoencoder is trained once, then frozen; only the U-Net trains
    during diffusion.
  - The VAE provides the space; diffusion provides the generation intelligence.

LDM Architecture / Flow:
  - Pixel space: original input image x (e.g. 512x512x3 RGB) -> Encoder E
    compresses pixels into latent z -> Decoder D reconstructs latent to pixels
    -> reconstructed image x_hat returned to the user.
  - Latent space: compressed, lower-dimensional representation where diffusion
    actually runs; ~48x smaller than pixel space, making diffusion cheap.
    Forward (training) z -> z1 -> z2 -> z_T; Reverse (generation)
    z_T -> z_{T-1} -> ... -> z1 -> z.
  - The denoising U-Net eps_theta iteratively predicts noise and recovers a
    clean z from z_T. Q/K/V blocks are cross-attention layers inside the U-Net
    where conditioning signals are injected.

Conditioning:
  - External control signals that guide the U-Net during denoising. Without it
    generation is random; with it, generation is controllable.
  - Types: Semantic maps (segmentation masks, layout maps, scene graphs),
    Text (natural-language prompts, e.g. "a cat playing piano"), Representations
    (generic embeddings, class labels), Images (reference images for img2img /
    inpainting).

Cross-Attention — How Conditioning Reaches the U-Net:
  - Noisy latent z_t asks questions (Q); conditioning c provides answers (K, V).
  - Query comes from noisy latent z_t; Key and Value come from conditioning
    embedding c.
  - Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) * V, where d = dimension of
    query/key vectors.
  - Intuition: QK^T measures similarity between every latent position and every
    conditioning token; softmax turns similarities into weights; the weighted V
    blends conditioning content into the latent at each position.

CLIP — The Text Encoder Behind Stable Diffusion:
  - CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) is OpenAI's model that aligns
    text and images into a shared embedding space, making text-to-image
    generation possible.
  - Three stages:
     1. Encode both — text -> CLIP text encoder -> text embedding; image ->
        CLIP image encoder -> image embedding.
     2. Contrastive training — pull matching (text, image) pairs together, push
        non-matching pairs apart.
     3. Shared embedding space — after training, text and image embeddings live
        in the same coordinate system.

-------------------------------------
SECTION 4 — LDMs AS WEB-EXPOSED SERVICES (Slides 21-24)
-------------------------------------
Cloud Deployment:
  - A typical production deployment wraps the model in a microservice
    architecture built for latency, scale, and safety.
  - Request flow: Client (browser UI / mobile app) -> Gateway (auth, rate
    limiting, routing) -> Inference Workers (GPU-backed, running the U-Net) ->
    Output (watermark + safety filters) -> returned image.
  - Real systems also add autoscaling (spin up GPU nodes on demand), logging
    and tracing (observability and debugging), and an asynchronous job queue
    for long-running workloads like video generation that can't fit inside a
    single HTTP request.

References (as listed in the deck):
  [1] Rombach et al. (2022). High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent
      Diffusion Models. CVPR 2022, pp. 10684-10695.
  [2] Podell et al. (2024). SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for
      High-Resolution Image Synthesis. ICLR 2024.
  [3] Stability AI (2023-2025). Stable Diffusion Developer Platform API Reference.
      developer.stability.ai
  [4] Hugging Face Diffusers Team (2025). Stable Diffusion Pipelines
      Documentation.
  [5] Shin, Kamyod & Hong (2026). Latent Diffusion Models: A Survey on
      Foundations, Variants, and Web-scale Deployments. Journal of Web
      Engineering 25(4), 599-634.
  [6] Hawkins, Mittelstadt & Russell (2025). Deepfakes on Demand. Proceedings
      of ACM FAccT '25.

-------------------------------------
KEY TAKEAWAYS
-------------------------------------
- LDMs move diffusion from pixel space into a compressed latent space, cutting
  compute by roughly 48x while retaining quality.
- A frozen VAE handles compression/reconstruction; the trainable U-Net performs
  the denoising in latent space.
- Conditioning (text, semantic maps, images, embeddings) is injected via
  cross-attention; CLIP is the standard text encoder.
- Production deployment requires a gateway, GPU inference workers, safety
  filters, autoscaling, observability, and async queues for long jobs.
